Antibiotic chemoprophylaxis is the principle of using antibiotics to prevent surgical site infections, morbidity and mortality.

**General Principles**:

- Assess risk of infection and need for prophylaxis (clean, contaminated, dirty surgery and patient factors/ comorbidities), clean surgery does not routinely require prophylaxis, not for treatment of infection. 
- Select the ideal agent and use in an appropriate way
- Work against the pathogens most likely to contaminate site, with consideration of their resistance patterns 
- Shortest effective durations 
- Correct administration to ensure optimal concentration during the procedure 
- Minimal adverse effects 
- Adverse drug reaction from the antibiotic 
- Selection pressure for resistant organisms
- Complications (such as Clostridium difficile infections and cannula site infections) 

**Cephazolin in joint replacement as an example:**

- Risk of infection moderate however morbidity associated with infection high as impacting prothesis into bone so antibiotic chemoprophylaxis indicated 
- Infection most likely from skin commensals including staphylococcal and streptococcal bacteria. 
- First generation cephalosporins (i.e. cephazolin) effective against skin commensal gram positive cocci, antibiotic child by be changed/influenced by presence or likelihood of resistant organisms i.e. MRSA
- Cephazolin is bactericidal
- Cephazolin IV formulation ideal for rapid delivery and absorption.  
- Dosage of cephazolin (25mg/kg) at least 15min but no longer than 60min prior to knife from skin / tourniquet inflation. 
- Duration 4 hours, repeat dose required in longer cases.
